3. The details of the ATNs are discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.

CHAPTER – I
RECOMMENDA TIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE
GOVERNMENT HA VE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
II.  BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation (para 2.11)
1.1 The Committee is of the opinion that keeping in view the mandate of DHR/ICMR to bring
modern technologies to the people through research and innovations and the fact that Department
has just launched the above mentioned Schemes to fulfill its mandate of creating a strong and
effective eco-system for carrying out health research in the country and for introduction of new
technologies, new methods of treatment and products/processes into the public health system; any
underfunding to the schemes would prove detrimental in achieving the desired objectives that too
at a time when these schemes have just picked up their pace. In view of the fact that with this
funds crunch it would not be possible for the Department to roll out many of its proposed
initiatives under the schemes, the Committee recommends that the Department should vigorously
pursue with the Ministry of Finance for enhanced funds at RE Stage. The Committee,
simultaneously, also recommends to the Department that it should take all out efforts for optimum
and judicious utilization of available resources and funds for implementation of various Schemes.
Funds for new initiatives should be limited to availability of funds.
Action Taken
1.2 As recommended by the Committee, efforts will also be made by the Department for
optimum utilization of the available funds, by taking following actions:
(i) The Department would impress upon the Ministry of Finance for making enhanced
allocations of funds at the RE stage for meeting the targets of the various schemes
in 2015-16.
(ii) While funding of new initiatives, preference will be given to the research projects/
proposals on health issues of national and public health importance, like, Cancer,
Cardio-vascular diseases, Diabetes, Maternal and Child Health, Nutritional
Deficiencies, V ector Borne Diseases, TB, Leprosy and Blindness control.
(iii)  Monthly monitoring to review the physical and financial progress of the schemes
will be done at the level of Joint Secretary to ensure efficient and effective
utilisation of budgetary allocations.
(iv) Similar review and monitoring on periodic basis will be done at the level of
Secretary, DHR.
(v) Conducting field visits to the medical colleges and institutions for reviewing the
progress of implementation of the schemes and making rational assessment of
requirement of funds.
2

3
III. INDIAN COUNCIL OF MEDICAL RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation (para 3.6)
1.3 The Committee puts on record its appreciation for ICMR for near optimum utilization of
allocated funds. Such a trend of utilization by the Institute would strengthen its demand for
additional funds at RE stage during the current year, as per the projections made. However, the
Committee would also like to say that mere utilization of funds is not an indicator of success,
unless the research outcomes are translated into health products or are used in better interest of
people. The Committee would like to be apprised of the steps being taken in speedy translation of
research leads into public utilities. The Committee would also like to be apprised of the number
of leads which were actually put into public use for their betterment.
Action Taken
1.4 The ICMR’s technologies/leads are shared with National Research Development Corporation
(NRDC) and Biotech Consortium India Limited (BCIL) under the Ministry of Science and
Technology, for technology transfer/commercialization.
1.5 The Division of Innovation & Translational Research (ITR) of ICMR is regularly following
up with the companies to review the progress. Through this process, eleven technologies have been
transferred to industries for commercialization.
Recommendation/Observation (para 3.11)
1.6 The Committee is happy to note that at its behest the Department has revisited its priorities
areas for research and drawn three most important priorities areas namely Cancer Research,
Environmental Health and Maternal and Child Health for carrying out research. The Committee is
hopeful that this move of the Department would result in visible and desirable results. The
Committee desires to be apprised of the outcome of the above move.
Action Taken
1.7 ICMR has constituted a core committee to develop cancer management guidelines of 20
specific types of cancers. Guidelines for 4 types of Cancers: Colorectal Cancer, Gall bladder
Cancer, Buccal Mucosa Cancer and Gastric cancer have been published and uploaded on the ICMR
website for public use. Guidelines for another 4 sites of cancers are in process of uploading on
the website.
1.8 ICMR has established the National Institute for Disease Informatics and Research, at
Bangalore for compiling the Cancer registries on national basis.
1.9 On the issues related to Environmental Health, ICMR has established the National Institute
for Research in Environmental Health (NIREH) at Bhopal.
1.10 On health issues related to air pollution, a Centre for Advanced Research has been
established in Chennai. The Centre has created a network of scientists across the country to
conduct research on households air pollution.
1.11 In the Maternal and Child Health (MCH), the priority areas of research are: reduction of
pre-natal and neonatal morbidities and mortalities; safe pregnancy and motherhood practices;

4
discovery of new, safe and acceptable contraception; reduction of respiratory (pneumonia) infection
in infants; polycystic ovarian syndrome diseases and better survival of low birth weight babies.
Recommendation/Observation (para 3.18)
1.12 The Committee appreciates the intervention made by the Department in the area of
environmental pollution and desires that research activities should not be restricted to air pollution
only as the health hazards of water/noise pollution are also affecting a large chunk of population.
Action Taken
1.13 Research activities of the National Institute of Occupational Health of ICMR, Ahmedabad
are not restricted to air pollution only and their thrust areas of research also include other
environmental hazards like, like noise pollution, water pollution thermal pollution and industrial
waste etc.

CHAPTER- II
RECOMMENDA TIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE
TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF  THE GOVERNMENT REPLIES
III. INDIAN COUNCIL OF MEDICAL RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation (para 3.20)
2.1 During the presentation on ICMR, the Committee was apprised about the network of ICMR
Institutes/Centres spread across the country. On a perusal thereof, the Committee noted that there
are regional imbalances in the presence of ICMR across the country. The Committee noted that a
large area of the Central India which also  happened to be tribal area which is malaria infected and
affected with various other environment-related morbidity factors is not covered under the projects
on traditional medicines. The Committee, accordingly, recommends to the Department to pay
attention in those areas which are not well served and seek additional resources for Eastern India
and Central India.
Action Taken
2.2 In addition to the existing Institutes/Centres of ICMR, the Department will be implementing
the 5 new schemes, viz. (1) Establishment of Multi-Disciplinary Research Units in Government
Medical Colleges, (2) Establishment of Model Rural Health Research Units in the States, (3)
Establishment of a Network of Laboratories for Managing Epidemics and Natural Calamities,
(4) Human Resource Development for Health Research and (5) Grant-in-Aid for Inter-sector
Convergence & Coordination for Promotion & Guidance on Health Research, which will result in
the opening of new centres/laboratories in central and eastern India and unserved areas.
IV. PROGRAMMES FOR THE NORTH EAST (NE)
Recommendation/Observation (para 4.3)
2.3 From a perusal of the initiatives proposed for NE region in the year 2015-16 vis-a-vis those
taken in the year 2014-15, the Committee notes that nothing new region specific programme has
been envisaged for the current year. The actual expenditure incurred vis-a-vis allocations made in
the year 2014-15 is also not very promising and reflects that many of the proposed initiatives
visualized for the year perhaps were either delayed or not accomplished. The Committee hence
exhorts that the Department may take all measures for optimum and judicious utilization of the
allocations made in the current financial year for the NE region.
Action Taken
2.4 During the year 2015-16, priority will be given to release the next instalment in respect of
the Multi-Disciplinary Research Units (MRUs) Viral Diagnostic & Research Laboratories and Model
Rural Health Research Units (MRHRUs) already sanctioned in the NE States.
Efforts will also be made to cover all the States/all the probable region in establishing the
Viral Diagnostic & Research Laboratories (VRDLs) and MRUs.
5

6
2.5 The following activities are also proposed in the North Eastern Region during  2015-16:
Bio medical Research Centre (BRC) of ICMR at Hengrabari, Guwahati is to be
constructed with an estimated cost of R47.58 Crores.
A Field Station of Regional Medical Research Centre, Dibrugarh is to be
established at Agartala (Tripura). A land measuring 3 acres has been acquired for this
purpose.
A Memorandum of Understanding has been signed between ICMR and
Government of Arunachal Pradesh to establish a Multi-Disciplinary Research Unit of
ICMR in  the Arunachal State Hospital, Naharlagun.
Beside the above stated new activity, ICMR has established
Multi- disciplinary Research Units at Falkawn, Mizoram and Kohima, Nagaland in 2014-15.
2.6 ICMR is also focusing on research activities on communicable diseases in the North
Eastern Region. A total of 35 research projects have been shortlisted, out of which 6 projects have
been initiated and remaining are awaiting technical/financial approval. Two Task Force studies on
neonatal sepsis and transmission of malaria infection employing newer technology at international
border areas will also be initiated in 2015-16.
VI. DEVELOPMENT OF INFRASTRUCTURE FOR PROMOTION OF HEALTH RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation (para 6.10)
2.7 The Committee desires that more States may be covered under the Scheme. The
Department may also set up more MRHRUs covering all the States.
Action Taken
2.8 Proposal will be formulated to scale up the programme in the 13
th Five Year Plan to cover
more States, based on the outcomes and success of the programme in the already sanctioned
MRHRUs.
VII. GRANT-IN-AID FOR INTER-SECT ORAL CONVERGENCE  & PROMOTION  AND
GUIDANCE ON HEALTH RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation (para 7.9)
2.9 The Committee apprehends that shortfall in allocations made for the Scheme would hamper
the pace of projects already initiated. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to
take all measures to offset impact of shortfall of allocations. Simultaneously, the Department
should also present a strong case for seeking more funds at RE Stage.
Action Taken
2.10 The Department would impress upon the Ministry of Finance for making enhanced
allocations of funds at the RE stage for meeting the targets of the various schemes in 2015-16.
2.11 As recommended by the Committee, efforts will also be made by the Department for
optimum utilization of the available funds to offset the impact of shortfall in allocations, by taking
following actions:

7
(i) priority will be given to meet the committed expenditure on the already sanctioned
projects/Units.
(ii) While funding of new initiatives, preference will be given to the research projects/
proposals on health issues of national & public health importance, like, Cancer,
Cardio-vascular diseases, Diabetes, Maternal & Child Health, Nutritional
Deficiencies, V ector Borne Diseases, TB, Leprosy and Blindness control.
(iii) Monthly monitoring to review the physical & financial progress of the schemes will
be done at the level of Joint Secretary to ensure efficient and effective utilisation
of budgetary allocations.
(iv) Similar review and monitoring on periodic basis will be done at the level of
Secretary, DHR.
(v) Conducting field visits to the medical colleges & institutions for reviewing the
progress of implementation of the schemes and making rational assessment of
requirement of funds.
(vi) Speedy release of grants to the medical colleges to improve the profile of utilisation
of budgetary allocations.
Recommendation/Observation (para 8.8)
2.12 The Committee is perturbed to find that the component for creation of the Revolving
fund to facilitate a rapid mobilization of outbreak/disaster response to infectious diseases
outbreak or a natural or man made disaster was not approved in the EFC meeting held under
the Chairmanship of Finance Secretary and Secretary of Expenditure. The Committee observes
that creation of such a fund was very vital for the country owing to recent outbreaks of
diseases like Swine Flu, Chikunguniya etc. As the Department has also expressed its inability
to establish a budget line to cater for the emergency action in case of infectious diseases
outbreak , the Committee recommends that the Department may approach the Ministry of
Finance for reviewing its decision in the matter.
Action Taken
2.13 The proposal to create a separate budget line for facilitating Emergency Relief & Rapid
Mobilization to combat out-breaks/disaster and response to infectious diseases, has already been
approved by Secretary, DHR.  Proposal is now being forwarded to the Budget Division of Ministry
of Finance for taking further necessary action.

CHAPTER – III
RECOMMENDA TIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE
GOVERNMENT HA VE NOT  BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
II. BUDGETARY PROVISIONS
Recommendation/Observation (para 2.3)
3.1 The Committee notes that on one hand the Department claims that significant progress has
been made in respect of Schemes while on the other the Committee notes that only a meagre
amount of expenditure of R179.36 crore upto 4.3.2015 could be made against the allocations of
R5213.00 crore made for the Schemes for Twelfth Plan Period. The Committee understands that
all the Schemes could be rolled in the year 2013-14 only and hence the expenditure booked was
very low. The Committee, however, is constrained to comment that this state of affairs indicates
that the Department was consistently over estimating its requirements and has not been able to
make use of scarce financial resources. The Committee, accordingly, impresses upon the
Department to make all out efforts to implement its proposed activities under the schemes in the
remaining two years of the Twelfth Five Year Plan for optimum utilization of allocations and for
achieving the desired objectives.
Action Taken
3.2 The Twelfth Plan allocation of R5213.00 crores for the five newly formulated schemes of
the DHR was based on the proposed estimated cost of each scheme. However, the final cost of
all the five schemes approved by the EFC/Cabinet worked out to be R3055.00 crores (approx.).
Against this, the actual budgetary allocation in the first four years (2012-13 to 2015-16) has been
to the extent of R677.00 crores only.
3.3 Allocation in 2012-13 for the schemes could not be utilised as the schemes could be finally
approved by the EFC/Cabinet in 2013-14. In fact, the two schemes, namely, (1) Human Resource
Development for Health Research and (2) Grant in aid scheme for Inter sectoral Convergence &
Promotion and guidance on Health Research were approved in February, 2014 only.
3.4 The Department has made its estimation meticulously at the time of finalization of Twelfth
Plan allocation for all the five schemes. However, while approving the schemes, the physical targets
were reduced, due to which the financial cost of the schemes came down from the original
proposed cost of R5213 crores to R3055 crores.
3.5 The schemes were rolled out for implementation immediately and the proposal were
processed for technical evaluation and final approval for release of fund in the same year. This was
possible only since pre-project actions had been taken by the Department in respect of all the five
schemes.
3.6 Depending upon the budgetary allocations, all efforts will be made by the Department to
implement the schemes by achieving maximum physical targets, through optimum utilization of
allocated resources.
8

9
Further Recommendation
3.7 The Committee does not find plausible the explanation given by the Department on
the formulation and approved procedure for the five schemes. Either the Department lacks
serious wherewithal to ensure timely formulation or approval of schemes or does not have
the vision to plan and implement schemes. The Committee seriously doubts whether these
schemes would be taken to their logical conclusion at the end of the Twelfth Five Year Plan
keeping in view the physical and financial progress made so far. The Committee, once again
recommends that the Department should identify and overcome the shortcomings in the
mechanism of budgetary planning so that the under-utilization of budgeted funds being
witnessed do not recur in the remaining years of the Twelfth Plan and the desired objectives
are not compromised.
Recommendation/Observation (para 2.6)
3.8 As evident from the above tables there are huge variations between the BE and RE for all
the schemes as well as for ICMR. The reasons cited by the Department for this trend were non-
receipt of adequate number of applications on account of approval of the scheme at fag end of
2013-14, pendency of utilization certificates, receipt of less number of proposals from States and
non-completion of requisite administrative and technical formalities under the Schemes guidelines by
certain States. The Committee, in the circumstances, is constrained to observe that inspite of its
repeated recommendations to the Department to take all out measures, including completion of pre-
project planning and formalities of obtaining necessary approvals for optimum and judicious
utilization of budgeted funds, not much has been done in this regard. The Committee fails to
understand the reasons for the delay in formulation of all the schemes even though the Schemes
first got in- principle approval by the Planning Commission in December 2010. The Committee is
not convinced with the statement of the Department that inspite of its best efforts, the various
actions like the appraisal of the Schemes, responding to various appraisal agencies, clearance of
the Schemes by EFC/CCEA took more than anticipated time which ultimately led to the delay. The
Committee observes that this is a clear case of lack of foresight and faulty planning by the
Department. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should make all possible
efforts with proper and timely planning to utilize the allocated funds at BE Stage. The Committee
would like to be apprised of the steps being taken or proposed to be taken to arrest this trend of
underutilization of budgeted funds which eventually led to massive cuts at RE stage.
Action Taken
3.9 The in-principle  approval of the Planning Commission to the Schemes was received in
December, 2010 i.e. in the midst of Eleventh Five Year Plan. The detailed EFC documents were
prepared and circulated by the Department for the comments of the appraisal agencies, soon
thereafter. However, since 2011-12 was the last year of the Eleventh Five Year Plan, the
Department was advised to formulate comprehensive schemes for the full Twelfth Plan period.
3.10 Hence, revision of EFC documents with modified cost estimates for the Twelfth plan period
and the process of obtaining approvals from the EFC and Cabinet took time and the schemes could
be finally approved in 2013-14 only.

10
3.11 The Department had already taken advance actions for inviting proposals from the States/
Medical Colleges, etc. and it was as a result of this action that it was possible to roll out and
implement all the five schemes during 2013-14 itself, alongwith the release of funds for the various
projects.
3.12 W ith a view to ensure optimum utilisation of allocated funds under the various schemes,
regular monitoring of physical/financial progress of the projects is being made through periodical
progress reports as well as  through onsite visits by the teams from DHR/ICMR. Review meetings
are also held at the level of Joint Secretary and Secretary (DHR) and action plan is formulated for
effective implementation of all the schemes and for utilisation of allocated funds.
Further Recommendation
3.13 The Committee would like to be apprised of the progress made in the actual
implementation of these five schemes and whether the intended objectives of the five
schemes would be achieved by end of the Twelfth Plan.
V . HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT FOR HEALTH RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation (para 5.6)
3.14 The Committee fails to understand as to why there was so much delay in implementing the
scheme which resulted in surrender of the entire budgeted funds for the year 2012-13 and drastic
reduction of allocations in RE 2013-14. Trained and qualified manpower is pre-requisite for
implementation of various research schemes of the Department. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department must complete all pre-project activities timely and properly to
avoid recurrence of the existing trend of underutilization. Allocation may be increased at RE stage,
if necessary, depending on the number of eligible proposals received. Publicity may be given to the
Scheme.
Action Taken
3.15 (1) Additional allocations, if considered necessary, will be sought at RE stage, depending
upon the number of applications for fellowships received and found edible for funding,
(2) The steps taken to improve the utilization of funds under the scheme include the following:
(i)  Letter has been addressed to the Principal Secretaries of Health & Family Welfare and
Directors of Medical Education of the States/UT, for giving wide publicity to the
scheme to attract adequate number of applications.
(ii) DHR will also give wide publicity through newspapers/websites for inviting applications.
3.16 The medical colleges/institutions will be impressed upon during various review meetings and
field visits by the officers to motivate the factually/researchers to avail the facilities under the
scheme.
Further Recommendation
3.17 The Committee recommends that this scheme should be given maximum importance
by the Department and would like to be apprised of the actual steps taken on ground to
enhance Human Resource Development for Health Research as Human Resource

11
Development is a key pillar for implementation of advances to be made in Health Research
which would in turn ensure incremental innovations to curb the various diseases plaguing
the country and also help in reducing costs for implementation of various Health
Programmes optimally.
VI. DEVELOPMENT OF INFRASTRUCTURE FOR PROMOTION OF HEALTH RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation (para 6.6)
3.18 The Committee observes that deaths caused due to non-communicable diseases are much
more than those occurring due to communicable diseases and any underfunding to the Scheme,
which promotes research in Non-Communicable diseases, will prove detrimental to control lifestyle
diseases. The proposed shortfall in allocation to the Scheme may lead to curtailment in the second
or subsequent installments to the Institutes where the Department has already made a beginning and
would result in seriously hampering of research activities initiated. The Committee, therefore, lends
its support to the demand of the Department for enhancement of allocations at RE Stage for the
Scheme so that investments already made in the medical colleges under the Scheme do not go
down the drain. The Committee finds that life style-related disease like hypertension, blood
pressure, diabetes etc. are on the rise and are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the
country and, therefore, it is a cause of serious concern. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the life style-related diseases may be included in the research programmes of the Department.
Action Taken
3.19 ICMR and the Medical Colleges will be requested to include life-style related diseases,
namely, diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular diseases, in their research programmes.
Further Recommendation
3.20 The Committee would like to be apprised of the specific steps taken by ICMR to
include lifestyle diseases in their research programmes.

GUIDANCE ON HEALTH RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation (para 7.8)
3.21 The Committee observes that some of very important activities are targeted to be
accomplished under the Scheme for Inter-Sectoral Convergence & Promotion and Guidance on
Health Research. The Committee is happy to note that pursuant to its recommendation made in 56th
Report and reiterated in 67th Report for creation of an institutional coordination mechanism for
synergizing the core competencies of the different organizations/agencies a group of Secretaries has
been constituted, consisting of Secretaries from DBT, DRDO, DARE/ICAR, ISRO, Department of
Space, DIT etc. to coordinate and collaborate on Health Research activities among various
departments. The Committee hopes that anticipated dividends are being accrued from this move.

held on 21st January 2014  and the Review Meeting of the Working Groups held on 12.08.2014

3.23 The concerned lead departments are required to take further actions for developing the joint
research projects in consultation with the other member departments.
3.24 Joint research projects will help in avoiding duplication of efforts and pooling of resources
for better outcomes and deliverables.

CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE
GOVERNMENT HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation
1.1 The Committee is concerned to find that there were savings of significant magnitude under
several important heads during 2013-14 and 2014-15 as is evident from Table Nos. 2 and 3 given
above. The fact that the savings were not just the result of implementation of economy measures
but occurred due to various reasons like non-filing of posts, non-approval of schemes, delay in
execution work, slow space of construction etc., clearly suggests that there were inadequacies in
the monitoring mechanism, as well as budgetary planning process and budget allocations were
proposed without obtaining all necessary clearances. The Committee is of the firm view that the
savings would have been minimized substantially if proper internal auditing and streamlined moni-
toring mechanisms had been in place and periodic review of the trends and progress of expenditure
had been adopted. The Committee notes that the Ministry of AYUSH has initiated, at the behest of
this Committee, a number of steps to ensure optimal and efficient utilization of allotted funds. The
Committee would like the Ministry to scrupulously implement the initiatives taken in this regard and
simultaneously evaluate the impact of new initiatives on utilization of budgeted funds. The Com-
mittee would like to be kept apprised of the impact of the new initiatives taken on utilization of
budgeted funds.   (Para 22)
Action Taken
1.2 The Department of AYUSH has become a full fledged Ministry w.e.f. 9.11.2014.  A number
of measures have been initiated, as suggested by the  Committee, to ensure efficient utilization of
allocated funds.  These initiatives have yielded significant improvement and accordingly, about 26%
of the allocated funds of R1,008/- crore (Plan) have been utilized as on 30.06.2015 which is a
substantial improvement in terms of percentage of expenditure as compared to previous years
(5%-6%) of this Ministry on corresponding date. Concerted efforts are being continued to improve
the expenditure further during the remaining period of the year 2015-16.
Recommendation/Observation
1.3 The Committee is constrained to note that there has been persistent and substantial
underutilization of Plan funds under the heads – “Hospitals and Dispensaries”, “Educational
Institutions”, “Research and Development including Medicinal Plants”, “Development of A YUSH
Industry”, and “National Mission on AYUSH”. The allocations made in BE 2013-14 and BE
2014-15 under the above heads, were subsequently revised downwards at the RE stage and the
sums which remained grossly underutilized, were surrendered by the end of the year. The
Committee observes that such huge variations in BE, RE and Actuals are indicative of the fact that
2

3
principles of fiscal prudence and discipline were neither observed nor proper assessment of the
projects was carried out. The Committee observes that in a resource-constrained country like India,
all care needs to be taken to ensure that the scarce resources do not remain locked up and
surrendered at the fiscal end. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry chalk out
its fiscal roadmap in such a way that the allocated funds are utilized optimally and more
productively under the above Heads and such a situation does not recur in future.    (Para 23)
Action Taken
1.4 The Ministry of AYUSH has initiated a number of steps to ensure optimal and efficient
utilization of allotted funds. The corrective measures taken  by this Ministry for better financial and
fiscal discipline have resulted in improvement in expenditure amounting to R258.96 crore which is
about 26% of BE of R1008 crore during the first quarter of the current Financial Year 2015-16
in comparison to R57.58 crore (5.39 per cent of BE of R1069 crore) in 2014-15 during the same
period.  Concerted efforts are being made to optimally utilize the funds under different heads.
Recommendation/Observation
1.5 The Committee observes that to obtain greater evenness in the budgeted expenditure
within a financial year and reduce rush of expenditure in the last quarter of the financial year,
Ministry of Finance has prescribed the expenditure ceiling of 33% for the last quarter of the
financial year. As is evident from Table No. 5, the Ministry of AYUSH has breached the ceiling
of 33%, though only marginally, by incurring expenditure of 36.61% of plan funds in the last
quarter. The Committee would like the Ministry to monitor expenditure of funds more closely
and avoid rush of expenditure in the last quarter.   (Para 25)
Action Taken
1.6 A proper monitoring mechanism has been put in place to review the expenditure
periodically to see the allocated funds are spent evenly in each quarter of the financial year
so that the rush of expenditure in the last quarter is avoided.  It may be mentioned that during
the current financial year, an amount of R258.96 has already been incurred against the budget
allocation of R1,008/- crore (Plan) upto 30.06.2015 which is about 26% which indicates the
proper pace of expenditure.
Recommendation/Observation
1.7 The Committee notes with concern that out of the plan allocation of R1069.00 crore
each in BE 2013-14, and BE 2014-15, as much as R507.99 crore and R573.21 crore were
surrendered in Financial Years 2013-14 and 2014-15 respectively. The Committee takes a
serious view of the fact that the Ministry kept unspent budgetary provisions of R507.99 crore
in 2013-14 and R573.24 crore in 2014-15 till the last day of the financial years despite
reduction in allocations at RE stage. The Committee observes that the unspent budgetary
provisions should have been surrendered as soon as these were foreseen without waiting till
the end of the Financial Year so that they could have been gainfully utilized under some other
heads. The Committee would like the Ministry to improve financial discipline.   (Para 26)

4
Action Taken
1.8 Noted for compliance.
CENTRALLY SPONSORED SCHEMES
Recommendation/Observation
1.9 The Committee observes that now that the National AYUSH Mission has been approved
and implemented, the Ministry should work out modalities in consultation with all the
stakeholders including the North Eastern States to ensure that utilization of the budgeted funds
for NE States does not suffer from any inadequacies and registers a marked improvement in
2015-16.   (Para 44)
Action Taken
1.10 Budget Estimate of R318.00 crore has been approved for the newly created scheme ‘NAM’
for stakeholders (State/UT) including the North Eastern States for 2015-16. Out of
R318.00 crore, there is a provision of R36.40 Crore for the North Eastern States, which is more
than normal rate of 10% of BE.
1.11 In this regard, Ministry of AYUSH already intimated the State/UT resource pool to the
States/UT Governments requesting them to send the State Annual Action Plan (SAAPs) by

2.33 In order to meet the  testing requirements of ASU&H drugs, the Ministry of A YUSH

th Five Year Plan, the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Quality Control of ASU&H

(UCs) or refund the unspent amount of grants released to them under the Centrally Sponsored

clear and remaining States have been repeatedly asked to settle the grant accounts without further
delay by submission of proper UCs and associated documents or refund the unspent amounts.
2.36 Following are the activities of drug quality control, which can be supported through
National AYUSH Mission-

16
(i) Strengthening of Ayurvedic, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathic drugs Pharmacies of
State Government/ Co-operatives/Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs.).
(ii) S trengthening/establishment of State Drug Testing Laboratories.
(iii) S trengthening of Ayurvedic, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathic drugs control frame
work.
(iv) Engagement of technical manpower in State Drug Testing Laboratories.
(v) Documentation, publication and dissemination of quality control materials.
(vi) Quality testing of drugs.
2.37 Minerals/metals are ingredients of a specific category of Ayurvedic drugs called
‘Rasaushadhies’. Quality standards of 21minerals/metals are published in the Ayurvedic
Pharmacopeia Pt. I, V ol.VII. These minerals are subjected to certain processes called Shodhana,
Marana, Amritikaran etc. for rendering them therapeutically safe and effective and it is mandatory
for the manufacturers to follow the pharmacopoeial standards and the Good Manufacturing
Practices (GMP) provided in the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules. Permissible limits of heavy metals
(Mercury, Lead, Cadmium, Arsenic), aflatoxins, pesticide residue, and microbial load are prescribed
in the Pharmacopeia and mandatory to be complied with herbal Ayurvedic drugs. The Ministry of
AYUSH have also issued orders since 2008 that drugs without adhering to permissible limits of
heavy metals may not be allowed for export and set up a Committee of Experts headed by Director
General of Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences to examine the incidences of alert/
ban and defaming articles in newspapers/journals about Ayurveda and formulate suitable rebuttal
response to protect the credibility of Ayurvedic system.  Ministry has also brought out Essential
Drug Lists of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy to facilitate states for procurement of
medicines from these lists with the grants provided through National AYUSH Mission.  Instructions
have been issued to the Central and State procurement regarding analytical reports of each batch
of the medicines supplied by the manufacturers to the dispensaries and hospitals. Spurious,
Misbranded and Adulterated ASU drugs are defined in the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and penalties
are prescribed for those, who act in contravention of the quality related provisions.  Individual
incidences of quality issues of ASU&H drugs brought to the notice of Ministry of AYUSH are taken
up with the state authorities for necessary action.

INFORMATION, EDUCATION AND COMMUNICATION
Recommendation/Observation
2.40 The Committee observes that despite the above steps taken by the Ministry the overall
standard of education in AYUSH colleges continues to be poor. The Committee therefore
recommends the Ministry to reorient its focus on improving the quality and standards of A YUSH
education in the country and regulating the same effectively. The Committee would like the Ministry
to have the accreditation standards of AYUSH Colleges prescribed by the Quality Council of India.
 (Para 128)
Action Taken
2.41 A yurveda, Siddha and Unani (ASU) education and systems of medicine are regulated under
the provisions of the Indian Medicine Central Council Act, 1970 (IMCC Act) and the relevant
regulations made thereunder. The Central Council of Indian Medicine (CCIM) is a statutory body
made under the IMCC Act to regulate the practice and education of these ASU systems of
medicine. There is no provision in the IMCC Act and its Regulations to follow any standard of any
other Act and Regulations prescribed by any other Council except CCIM. Therefore, it will be in
violation of IMCC Act and its Regulations to have the accreditation standards of AYUSH Colleges
prescribed by the Quality Council of India.
2.42 It is pertinent to mention here that the CCIM is the only regulatory authority to prescribe
the standards of education and infrastructure of ASU Colleges by the way of notifications with the
prior approval of the Central Government. All the Gazette notifications of subordinate legislations
published by the CCIM are laid down on both the tables of Parliament (Rajya Sabha and Lok
Sabha) as per the provisions of the Act.  Hence, the Quality Council of India cannot prescribe the
standards of education and infrastructure of ASU Colleges and a college cannot follow the two
different standards at the same time.
2.43 The CCIM has made a number of Regulations to regulate the quality education in ASU
systems at undergraduate and postgraduate levels. The Council is revising from time to time the
course and curriculum of study in ASU Colleges as per the recommendations of the various
committees of the expert set up for the purpose. The suggestions from different forums, experts
and stake holders are also invited and incorporated in preparation and amendment of the Regulations
and curriculum. Any new Regulation or amendment is also circulated by the Council to all State
Governments for their comments before notification.  A list of CCIM’s Regulations and
amendments made so far to regulate and improve the quality education of Ayurveda, Siddha and
Unani (ASU) systems of medicine can be seen at Annexure-B.
2.44 Presently, there are 334 ASU Colleges with annual intake capacity of 21004 students (17628
UG + 3376 PG) (281 Ayurveda Colleges with 15087 under-graduate seats and 3089
post-graduate seats, 9 Siddha Colleges with 410 under-graduate seats and 140 post-graduate seats
and 44 Unani Colleges with 2131 under-graduate seats and 147 post-graduate seats).

QUALITY CONTROL OF ASU&H DRUGS
Recommendation/Observation
3.32 The Committee observes that quality control and standardization of ASU&H drugs leaves
much to be desired. It has often been reported in the media that Ayurveda and Homoeopathy drugs,
which were given to patients for various ailments, were laced with steroids and other improper
drugs. Permissible limits of heavy metals, pesticide residue, microbial load etc. are also sometimes
breached and regulatory needs of standardization and quality control of ASU&H drugs get seriously
impaired. On the issue of setting up of a separate Drug Controller of AYUSH, the decision to
develop a vertical structure of AYUSH in the present Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation
(CDSCO) headed by the Drug Controller General of India is not acceptable to the Committee. The
Committee feels that in order to strengthen regulatory mechanism and effectively oversee the
quality control of ASU&H drugs, setting up of a separate Central Drug Controller for ASU&H drugs
is an imminent necessity since a wing of AYUSH in the existing CDSCO may not produce the
desired result of effective regulation of ASU&H drugs. The Committee is of the view that a
separate Central Drugs Controller of AYUSH will help synergise the core competencies of the
Central and State Regulatory Authorities by developing dynamic relation between them and also go
a long way in building credibility in ASU&H drugs besides promoting AYUSH in foreign countries.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that action be initiated to set up an independent and
separate Central Drug Controller for ASU&H drugs at the earliest.  (Para 108)
Action Taken
3.33 The Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules thereunder provide licensing and enforcement
powers to the State Governments for Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homeopathic (ASU&H) drugs.
The Central Government makes and amends the legal provisions for ASU&H drugs, which are
enforced by the State Governments and support is provided for strengthening of enforcement
framework in the States.  The proposal of a separate Central Drugs Controller General of India
for AYUSH aimed at overseeing the implementation of regulatory provisions for ASU&H drugs in
the country was moved on the basis of recommendations of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani Drugs
Consultative Committee since 2010.  The objective is to develop improved coordination between
Central and State Regulatory Authorities for quality control of ASU&H drugs and facilitate effective
supervision over enforcement of the provisions of Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the Rules,
1945 pertaining to Ayurvedic, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy drugs. Recently, Government has
considered to set up a structured central regulatory regime for AYUSH medicines and the current
proposal is to have a vertical structure for AYUSH in the Central Drugs Standard Control
Organization (CDSCO). Government has initiated procedural steps for setting up the vertical
structure of AYUSH in the CDSCO and the need for creation of a separate Drugs Controller
General for AYUSH may be assessed subsequently, the time-frame for which cannot be specified
at this stage.   The draft Recruitment Rules for the posts agreed by the Department of Expenditure
are in the process of approval for onward transmission to Department of Health & Family Welfare.
Further Recommendation
3.34 The Committee reiterates its recommendation and desires to know the final outcome
in the matter.
Recommendation/Observation

th Report on Demands for Grants 2012-13, had commented upon

th Report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee, Department of Health
& Family Welfare, under whose jurisdiction Task Force for suggesting amendments in the Drugs

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family
Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf present this Ninety-
second Report of the Committee on the Functioning of Medical Council of India (MCI).
2. The previous Committee had identified the subject ‘Medical  Council of India’ at its meeting held on
18th September, 2014. However, it could not conclude its examination of the subject. The present Committee
also took up the subject for detailed examination at is meeting held on 23rd September, 2015.
3. The Committee examined the subject, in its sittings held on 25th September, 2014,  28th January,
2015, 12th May, 2015, 25th May, 2015, 27th July, 2015, 6th October, 2015 and 1st March, 2016. During
the course of the examination it took oral evidences of representatives of the Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare and experts on the subject.  The Committee also received written submissions from experts. The
Committee wishes to appreciate the  contribution made by various official witnesses/experts (Annexures I
and II) who richly deserve Committee’s encomia for sharing their perspectives and valuable views with the
Committee and suggesting remedies to the problems afflicting Medical Education and Practice in the country
through their evidences and written submissions. The Committee also benefited  from discussions with
certain stakeholders and representatives of the State Governments during its study visit to Tamil Nadu and
Karnataka from 8th June to 12th June, 2015 and local study visit to Vardhaman Mahavir Medical College
(VMMC), New Delhi and Shri Guru Govind Singh Tercentenary Medical College (SGGSTMC), Gurgaon on
the 2nd February, 2016.
4. The Committee had also invited views from various stakeholders in response to which 46 Memoranda
had been received (Annexure-III). The Memoranda were forwarded to the Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare for comments which informed the Committee that the  same had been forwarded to the MCI which
has formed a Committee to examine the issues raised in the memoranda. The President, MCI informed that
the report is already prepared and has passed through EC (Executive Committee) and now will go to GB
(General Body) in March, 2016. On a direction by the Committee to expedite the said GB body meeting, the

MCI.

REPORT
CHAPTER–I
BACKGROUND
1.1 Despite having the most number of medical colleges in the world, and currently having approximately
9.29 lakhs doctors enrolled on the Indian Medical Register, India is way behind in achieving the targeted
doctor population ratio of 1:1000 as per WHO norms. Shortage of doctors, who are the most important
cog in the health care delivery system, has derailed both access to and quality of health care, especially
to the vulnerable and poorer sections of the country.
1.2 Though there have been substantial improvements in health outcomes over the years, there are still
large gaps in health care accessibility in many parts of the country and Universal Health Care still remains
a distant dream. Issues concerning medical education, access to adequate health care to all people and
the entrenched inadequacy of health and clinical governance in the country have been engaging the
attention of the Committee for quite some time. The Committee has been given to understand that the
following issues have been widely debated in various fora across the country:
i. failure of the current system to produce doctors including specialists and super specialists
in adequate numbers and of requisite quality;
ii. deficiency of teachers in medical colleges;
iii. poor regulation of Undergraduate (UG) and Postgraduate (PG) education;
iv. disconnect between medical education system and health system;
v. opacity in the functioning of the existing regulatory body of medical education ( i.e. Medical
Council of India);
vi. lack of accountability of Medical Council of India (MCI);
vii. geographical mal-distribution of medical colleges;
viii. failure of the MCI in discharging its mandated responsibilities;
ix. allegations of rampant corruption in the MCI;
x. constitution and composition of the MCI;
xi. absence of proper screening and admission procedures in private medical colleges;
xii. need for common entrance test for admissions to MBBS,Postgraduate and Super-specialty
medical courses;
xiii. prevalence of capitation fee in private medical colleges in flagrant violation of the law;
xiv. barriers to expansion of medical education;
xv. lack of a robust accreditation system for UG and PG Medical education;

2
xvi. gross inequity between rural and urban India in terms of availability of health care services;
xvii. ethical issues;
xviii. need for reforms in the regulatory framework of medical education and practice;
xix. over-investigation and over-treatment in private hospitals;
xx. inadequacy of self-regulatory processes for medical profession.
1.3 Since the Medical Council of India is mandated to play a pivotal role in regulating medical
education and practice in the country, the Committee decided to holistically examine its role and functioning
with the ultimate aim of suggesting veritable solutions to the inadequacies that are currently plaguing our
medical education and health care delivery systems.
1.4 At the initial stage of examination of the subject, the Committee called for a background note on
the functioning of Medical Council of India (MCI) from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
Background of MCI furnished by Ministry
1.5 The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in the background note submitted to the Committee
stated that the Medical Council of India was established in 1934 under the Indian Medical Council Act,
1933, with the main function of establishing uniform standards of higher qualifications in medicine and
recognition of medical qualifications in India and abroad. The Act was repealed and replaced by a new
Act in 1956. The Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 was further amended in 1964, 1993, 2001.
Organization Chart of MCI
(i) According to the Ministry, the following is the organization chart of MCI.


3
Objectives:
(ii) The Ministry stated that the Council has the following objectives:
(a) Maintenance of uniform standards of medical education, both under graduate and postgraduate.
(b) Recommendation for recognition/de-recognition of medical qualifications of medical institutions
of India or foreign countries.
(c) Permanent registration/provisional registration of doctors with recognized medical
qualifications.
(d) Reciprocity with foreign countries in the matter of mutual recognition of medical qualifications.
Functions and Duties:
(iii) As per the note submitted by the Ministry the following are the functions and duties of the Council:
(a) Permission to establish a new medical college or opening of a new or higher course of study
or training or increase in admission capacity in any course of study or training, including
exercise of power to finally approve or disapprove the same.
(b) Inspection/visitation with a view to maintain minimum standard of medical education in
India.
(c) Recognition/de-recognition of
(i) Indian Qualifications
(ii) Foreign Qualifications
(d) Registration
(i) Permanent Registration
(ii) Provisional Registration
(iii) Registration of Additional Qualifications
(iv) Issue of Good Standing Certificates to doctors going abroad
(v) Issue of Eligibility Certificate to candidates going abroad for pursuing primary medical
qualifications.
(e) Indian Medical Register: Maintenance of an Indian Medical Register of persons who hold
any of the recognized medical qualification or for the time being registered with any of the
State Medical Councils or Medical Council of India.
Further Amendments to the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956:

CHAPTER-II
STATE OF AFFAIRS IN HEALTH SYSTEMS AND CHALLENGES IN THE
DELIVERY OF HEALTH SERVICES IN THE COUNTRY
2.1 The Committee would, at the outset like to assess the state of affairs in health care delivery systems
in the country, for, medical education cannot be seen as an end in itself, but should be geared and attuned to
providing general, appropriate, accessible and affordable healthcare to all countrymen.
Access to Health Care Services
2.2 Though India has made considerable progress towards improving healthcare indicators such as life
expectancy, child mortality, maternal and infant mortality over the years, yet the outreach and services
delivery for the urban and rural poor has been inadequate and the gaps in health outcomes continue to widen.
2.3 “Despite being home to 17·5% of the global population, India accounted for 20% of the global burden
of disease in 2013 - only a slight improvement from 21% in 2005. India accounts for 27% of all the neonatal
deaths and 21% of all the child deaths (younger than 5 years) in the world. Diarrhoea, pneumonia, preterm
birth complications, birth asphyxia, and neonatal sepsis account for 68% of all deaths in children younger
than 5 years in the country.” 1
2.4 The following paragraph, which is an extract from the Report of the Group of Experts constituted by
the Ministry to study the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 highlights the magnitude of the gaps in our
healthcare services:-
“While many important healthcare indices, such as life expectancy, infant and maternal mortality
have improved significantly since independence, we lag woefully behind developed countries and
even other countries with similar socio economic status as ours, in these indicators. India’s Under
5 Child Mortality (Probability of dying before reaching age of 5 per 1000 live births) as in 2011
was 61, as compared to Nepal 50, Bhutan 54, Bangladesh 46, Peru 18, Maldives 15, China 15,
Brazil 16, Thailand 12, Sri Lanka 12, Chile 9, USA 8, Cuba 6, UK 5, Japan 3 and is slightly better
than only Pakistan 88. Maternal Mortality figures (number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live
births) are worse: India 200, Bhutan 180, Nepal 170, Brazil  56, Thailand 48, Sri Lanka 35, China
37, Chile 25 as compared to  USA 21, UK 12, Japan 5, Singapore 3.”
2.5 As per written submissions furnished by the experts, India faces a high degree of inequity in access
to health care services. There are urban-rural inequities and there are also geographical inequities. With rapid
privatization of medical education and healthcare since the 1980s, around 70% of medical professionals
work in the private health sector and around 70% of these are concentrated in urban well-to-do areas. As per
an article published in the Lancet, “a consequence of the insufficient reach of the public sector has been the
growth of a massive, heterogeneous and mostly unregulated private health-care sector. In 2014, more than
70% of outpatient care (72% in the rural areas and 79% in the urban areas) and more than 60% of inpatient
care (58% in rural areas and 68% in urban areas) was in the private sector.... Private practitioners are now
therefore the first point of contact in both rural and urban areas for many ailments, including fevers and
acute illnesses, care of neonates, and treatment of diseases such as tuberculosis. However, a substantial
proportion of, and in some areas even the majority of private providers might be unqualified or under-

7

8
qualified. For example, a study in rural Madhya Pradesh found that only 11% of the sampled health-care
providers had a medical degree, and only 53% of providers had completed high school Informal care
providers, with no formal medical training or registration with Government for medical practice, are estimated
to represent 55% of all providers and are also frequently the first point of contact, especially in rural areas.”
2
2.6 The major source of professional healthcare for rural and also many urban poor households is through
the public sector which is insufficient in infrastructure, human resources, equipment and drugs (especially
at the primary level). The first point at which a doctor is available in rural public health system is at the
Primary Health Centre (PHC) and there are 25308 PHCs
3 as on 31st March, 2015 for a rural population of
83.3 crore plus. This is just a drop in the ocean. These PHCs suffer from staff shortages. The shortfall of
allopathic doctors at PHCs as compared to requirement based on existing infrastructure is 11.9%3 “Moreover,
as compared to requirement for existing infrastructure, there was a shortfall of 83.4% of surgeons, 76.3%
of obstetricians & gynaecologists, 83.0% of physicians and 82.1% of paediatricians. Overall, there was a
shortfall of 81.2% specialists at the CHCs as compared to the requirement for existing CHCs.”
3
2.7 There has been a steady increase in vacancies in the positions of doctors at Primary Health Centres
over the last five to ten years (27% in 2015)
3 and an even more shocking increase in the vacancies of
specialists at secondary facilities. “The current position of specialists manpower at CHCs reveal that as on
31st March, 2015, out of the sanctioned posts, 74.6% of Surgeons, 65.4% of obstetricians & gynaecologists,
68.1% of physicians and 62.8% of paediatricians were vacant. Overall 67.6% of the sanctioned posts of
specialists at CHCs were vacant.” 4 Thus, there are very few surgeons, anesthetists, gynecologists and
paediatricians in the public health system, and people who live far from cities and towns have no option but
to travel long distances to avail surgical care.
2.8 Explaining about the status of health services in the country, Dr. Devi Shetty, Former Member, BoG,
MCI who deposed before the Committee on 27th July, 2015 submitted that:
“I am not really that concerned about the medical education but I am very concerned about the
impact it has on the lives of common people of this country. Every ten minutes a pregnant lady
dies during child birth and ten lakh children die within the first year of life. Why?” It is because
the common hospital these people approach, is the community health centre which takes care of
the health of 1,54,512 people.”
2.9 The strong link between poverty and ill health is a documented fact. According to the Government’s
draft National Health Policy 2015, “over 63 million persons are faced with poverty every year due to health
care costs alone. People have no financial protection for the vast majority of health care needs. In 2011-12,
the share of out-of-pocket expenditure on health care as a proportion of total household monthly per capita
income was 6.9% in rural areas and 5.5% in urban areas. This led to an increasing number of households
facing catastrophic expenditure due to health costs (18% of all households in 2011-12 as compared to 15%
in 2004-05).” Public funding is estimated to be of the order of only 19.67% of the expenses of health care
in the country (as per National Health Accounts Estimates-2004-05) and most of private expenditure is out-
of-pocket (OOP) expense, which has the potential of pushing even the non-poor into poverty. This clearly
indicates that the expansion of medical education has not fulfilled the increasing health needs of the people.

2.10 The Committee observes that though there have been substantial improvements in certain
health outcomes, especially in life expectancy, maternal and infant mortality, these achievements
should not mask India’s failures in achieving the desired level of health care delivery. As per the
Report of the Working Group on Tertiary Care Institutions for the Twelfth Five Y ear Plan, rates of
infant and maternal deaths still remain high, nearly one million Indians die every year due to
inadequate healthcare facilities, 700  million people have no access to specialist care and 80% of
specialists are working in urban areas. Despite India’s economy today being one of the world’s
fastest growing and third largest in terms of Gross National Health Income, our health system
continues to face a huge need gap in terms of access to adequate healthcare and availability of
health professionals and facilities. India also has the dubious distinction of lagging behind countries
like Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Peru, Maldives, China, Brazil, Thailand, Srilanka and Chile on
important health indicators including child mortality and maternal mortality. If 63 million persons
are faced with poverty every year due to health care costs alone (as per Draft National Health
Policy, 2015), it clearly indicates that health care is moving away from the reach of the people in
general and the poor in particular. This also indicates that India has not been able to leverage its
economic growth to achieve the desired health outcomes. The fact that there is an acute shortage of
doctors in the country and the effective delivery of health care services cannot be guaranteed
without the availability of doctors in adequate numbers, testifies to the point that the system of
medical education, as regulated by the Medical Council of India, has not been able to address the
many unmet health care needs of our health system and needs reforms urgently.
Shortage and uneven distribution of Doctors
2.11 The Committee has been informed by an expert that in large measure, the failure to improve the health
of our people is strongly linked to failure to expand the trained human resource- both in quantity and quality.
2.12 In a reply to a question the Ministry has informed the Committee that as per MCI records there are
9.29 lakh doctors registered in the Indian Medical Register as on 31.03.2014. Assuming 80% availability, it
is estimated that around 7.4 lakh doctors may be actually available for active service. It gives a doctor-
population ratio of 1:1674 against the WHO norm of 1:1000. At present, every year around 55000 doctors
and 25,000 PG doctors are passing out from various colleges. At this rate of growth, the country should
have a doctor (allopathic)- population ratio of 1:1250 for a population of 133 crores by 2020 and 1:1075 by
2022 (population: 136 crores). However, the Committee has been informed by an expert who deposed
before the Committee that doctors cannot be produced overnight and if we add 100 medical colleges every
year for the next five years, only by the year 2029, will the country have adequate number of doctors.
2.13 The following observation made by the Group of Experts constituted to study the IMC Act on 1956,
outlines the inadequacy of availability of medical professionals in India:-
“India has significantly lower numbers of doctors, nurses, midwives, community health workers and other
allied groups for health care delivery, as compared to the recommended global norms. The shortfall of
doctors is in spite of the massive expansion in the number of medical colleges, from 23 in 1947 to the
current 398; the total number of medical seats in 2014 is 49,930. As of 2010-11, India has only 6.5 doctors
per 10,000 of population, as compared to 17.6 in Brazil, 14.6 in China, 27.7 in UK, and 24.2 in USA. This is
far short of the global average and even below the target of 1 for 1000 of population recommended by the
High Level Expert Group Report on Universal Health Coverage for India”.

10
2.14 The then Health Secretary during deposition before the Committee admitted that the doctor population
ratio in India vis-a-vis WHO norm was indeed abysmal. He further submitted that it takes more than R 200
crore to set up a medical college and about R1500 crore to set up an AIIMS and because of resource
constraints, it was not possible to set up enough medical colleges and AIIMS-like institutions to take care of
the backlog.
2.15 The representative of the IMA during evidence tendered before the Committee submitted that India’s
assessment of requirement of doctors was based on the western concept where a specialist hardly sees 15
patients per day. In India even a general practitioner sees 500-1000 patients daily. He suggested that the
manpower requirement should be assessed assuming that a doctor sees 50-100 patients daily.
2.16 An expert who appeared before the Committee submitted that India was very very short of doctors
and to meet this shortfall, India needs to have not four hundred, but one thousand medical colleges.
2.17 The representative of the MCI during evidence informed the Committee through a power-point
presentation that there were 9.29 lakh doctors that were registered on the Indian Medical Register. When
asked whether this figure also included doctors who had gone abroad, the representative of the MCI replied
in the affirmative. When further asked about the actual number of doctors practicing in India, the representative
stated that the process to collect such data had been undertaken. The Joint Secretary who was present
during the evidence informed the Committee that those doctors who studied here and moved out were not
captured in the figures.
2.18 Besides acute shortage of medical doctors, there are serious issues concerning mal-distribution of
doctors and imbalanced growth of medical colleges in the country. In reply to a question, the Joint Secretary
of the Ministry during evidence submitted that “the capacity that we are seeing on UG and PG seats, almost
sixty five per cent is concentrated in the South and the West of the country. So, the deficit areas are really
the north and the East of the country.” The Health Secretary, who was also present during the deposition
informed that the doctors were distributed in an uneven manner and ensuring that the doctor goes to rural
areas remains a challenge and for that several measures have been taken.
2.19 Some experts who deposed before the Committee pointed out that:
(i) “there was a lot of geographical mal-distribution of medical colleges with clustering in some
parts and lacking in others.”
(ii) “We are unable to meet this demand and supply mismatch because the Medical Council of
India is standing as a big barrier in the development of new medical colleges and the same
thing applies to the geographical mal-distribution…”. He also informed the Committee that
“Six States which represent 31 per cent of India’s population have 58% of the MBBS seats;
on the other hand eight States which comprise 46% of India’s population have 21% of the
MBBS seats.”
(iii) “We have to decentralize health care manpower planning from the Centre to the State
Governments. Each State Government should get one of the top global consultancy firms
and find out what is the requirement of specialists, nurses, paramedics, etc.”
(iv) “health being a State subject, the planning for having adequate number of doctors should
be the State’s responsibility. The States should open new medical colleges and raise funds

11
for the purpose.”
2.20. During the Committee’s study visit to Coimbatore, Ooty and Bengaluru some of the stakeholders
suggested that to address the issue of uneven distribution of medical colleges in the country, the Central
Government should fund medical colleges in areas where there are very few medical colleges.
2.21 The Committee agrees that there is an acute shortage of medical doctors in the country
besides their geographical mal-distribution. The Committee takes note of the submission of Ministry
of Health and Family Welfare that the total number of doctors registered on the Indian Medical
Register is 9.29 lakhs out of which 7.40 lakhs are available for active practice and that the doctor -
population ratio in India is 1:1674 as against the WHO norm of 1:1000. However, given the fact that
the Indian Medical Register is not a live database and contains names of doctors who may have
passed away or retired from active practice, by now, as well as those with a permanent address
outside India and that there is no mechanism in place for filtering out such cases, the Committee is
highly sceptical of the Ministry’s claim of having one doctor per 1674 population. In view of the
above, the Committee feels that the total universe of doctors in India is much smaller than the
official figure and we may have one doctor per 2000 population, if not more. The Committee observes
that the imbalances in availability of affordable and quality health care cannot be corrected without
augmenting the capacity of production of medical doctors including specialists and super-specialists
in adequate numbers and of requisite quality and competence. Apart from the unfinished agenda of
communicable diseases, India is witnessing the rapidly rising burdens of non-communicable diseases
(Cardiovascular diseases, Cancer, Diabetes, Chronic respiratory disorders, Mental illness, Liver
and Kidney diseases), which call for the availability of many more category of doctors and specialist
doctors. The Committee is constrained to observe that the MCI has been unresponsive to health
system needs with the result that shortage in number of basic doctors and specialists, mal- distribution
of medical colleges and doctors across the States continue to plague the delivery of effective and
equitable health services. At the present rate of production of doctors, the shortfall in basic and
specialist doctors will not be met for many years. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
urgent measures may be taken to spell out policy stance in great detail and with clarity to augment
the capacity of production of doctors including specialists and super-specialists at the scale and
speed required to meet India’s health needs.
2.22 The Committee is concerned to note that the medical colleges in the country are distributed
in a skewed manner, with nearly sixty five per cent medical colleges concentrated in the Southern
and Western States of the country which has resulted in great variation in doctor-population ratio
across the States. The States of North, North-East and Central India have a severe shortage of
doctors because of very few medical colleges they have. The Committee also notes with concern the
that six States with 31% of India’s population account for 58% of the MBBS seats, while eight
States which comprise 46% of India’s population have 21% of the MBBS seats. The Committee is of
the opinion that the mere increase in medical seats to enable correction of this doctor-population
imbalance will not automatically address this skew because experience shows that doctors normally
settle in the cities they go to for their medical education and do not return to serve in their own
urban or rural areas. Also, even if compulsory rural service is introduced throughout India, graduates
of each State would be required to serve only in their State, as per present State health regulations,

12
and the States with very few medical colleges would continue to be disadvantaged. The Committee
would, therefore, recommend that an institutional mechanism be put in place to ensure better
distribution of medical colleges across the country. State level doctor-population ratio should guide
the setting up of new medical colleges and also the increase in UG and PG seats.
2.23 The Committee also observes that the present approach in the matter of healthcare manpower
planning is a top-down one. Since health is a State subject and State Governments are major
stakeholders in the delivery of healthcare services, medical manpower planning should be bottom-
up also. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that each State should plan for an optimal number
of doctors, with a target of 1:1000 doctor-population ratio.
